strengths: The paper proposes an interesting and potentially useful bridge between spectral graph methods and divide-and-conquer numerical linear algebra: representing the GFT via a sequence of Cauchy-like factors induced by rank-one Laplacian edge updates. The local-to-global framing is original and could be valuable for spectral GNNs on modular graphs.

The manuscript gives a coherent high-level algorithmic story: local eigendecompositions, hierarchical merging through Cauchy factors, and learnable spectral filters at local and global levels. The synthetic timing experiments support the claimed qualitative scaling with graph size and interface size in favorable settings.

The empirical results are competitive on the Platonov et al. heterophily/long-range benchmarks, with especially strong Minesweeper performance and a much smaller parameter count than transformer-style baselines. The paper also includes useful hyperparameter details and reports preprocessing runtimes.

The limitations of the approach are at least partly acknowledged: the dependence on small interfaces, the need for sparsification on dense cuts, and the fact that the method is most suitable when long-range dependencies and hierarchical/modular structure are relevant.
weaknesses: Several central technical claims need stronger justification. The theory is derived for combinatorial Laplacians under rank-one edge insertions, but the experiments use the normalized Laplacian. Adding an edge to a normalized Laplacian changes the degree normalization and is not simply a rank-one update of the previous normalized Laplacian. The statement that the factorization applies identically after normalization is not sufficient to support the experimental/theoretical connection.

The interface sparsification theorem appears overstated or incorrect as written. Sparsifying each cut/interface independently does not automatically imply the advertised global quadratic-form preservation without a careful compositional argument, and the proof inconsistently states both O(n log n/epsilon^2) and O(epsilon^-2) edges per interface. The claimed O(n log n) construction time also ignores the cost of estimating effective resistances.

The exact factorization result is conceptually interesting but partly follows from known rank-one symmetric eigenproblem updates; the paper does not fully separate what is novel mathematically from a composition of existing secular-equation/Cauchy update identities. Some details are shaky, e.g. Algorithm 3 omits the final secular root interval beyond the largest eigenvalue and glosses over repeated eigenvalues/zero projections in the actual solver.

The empirical evidence is too narrow for the strength of the claims. Real-world experiments use only four transductive datasets and apparently a one-level partition, while the method is motivated as a hierarchical framework. There are no ablations over hierarchy depth, sparsification ratio, partition quality, normalized vs combinatorial Laplacian, or approximation error relative to the exact GFT.

The reported accuracy gains are modest: the method is clearly best only on Minesweeper, trails Polynormer on three of four datasets, and is close to Stable-ChebNet. The parameter-count comparison is favorable but does not by itself establish better practical efficiency, since dense spectral transforms and preprocessing costs may dominate.

Runtime evaluation is incomplete. Table 2 compares eigendecomposition and Cauchy factorization preprocessing time, but not end-to-end training/inference time, memory footprint, GPU behavior, or the cost of repeatedly applying the learned spectral layers. Since the method remains quadratic and uses dense factors, scalability beyond these medium-sized graphs is not convincingly demonstrated.

Reproducibility is only partial. Hyperparameters and some implementation details are provided, but there is no clear code-release statement, no detailed random seed protocol, limited statistical testing, and insufficient details to reproduce numerical secular solvers, deflation handling, and sparsification robustly.

Presentation is generally readable, but important claims are sometimes imprecise or overstated. For example, the paper alternates between exact factorization and heavily sparsified approximate operation, and the relationship between the two in the reported GNN results is not made sufficiently explicit. Ethical concerns are minimal for these benchmark experiments, but broader limitations and failure modes are not deeply discussed.

strengths: The paper tackles a meaningful problem: reducing the cost and improving the locality of spectral GNNs based on graph Fourier transforms, which is relevant for long-range graph tasks.
The idea of composing local eigenspaces through rank-one/Cauchy updates is interesting, and the manuscript makes a serious attempt to connect numerical linear algebra with GNN design.
The synthetic runtime experiments are useful for illustrating the intended scaling behavior with graph size and interface size.
The model is parameter-efficient relative to transformer-style baselines, and the reported performance is broadly competitive on the selected heterophilous graph benchmarks.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claims are not fully convincing. The paper claims an exact factorization for arbitrary graphs and practical quadratic-time computation, but the argument depends heavily on favorable hierarchical partitions and small interfaces. For arbitrary graphs, the proposed remedy is aggressive sparsification, which changes the graph and no longer supports the same exact-GFT claim.

The treatment of normalized Laplacians appears under-justified. The theory is developed for combinatorial/generalized Laplacians with edge insertions as rank-one updates, while experiments use the normalized Laplacian. Adding an edge to a normalized Laplacian changes degrees and is not simply the same rank-one update structure; the appendix assertion that the results apply after normalization is too terse for such a central issue.

The interface sparsification theorem and proof are weak. The manuscript applies Spielman-Srivastava-style guarantees locally to interfaces, but the proof does not adequately justify preservation of the full graph spectral layer or the claimed construction cost. There are also inconsistencies between stated edge bounds and the proof sketch, and the practical experiments use up to 99.5% edge sparsification without a careful approximation-error study.

The empirical evidence is limited and does not strongly support the paper’s claims. On the four real-world datasets, the method is not clearly state of the art: it is worse than Polynormer on Roman-Empire, Amazon-Ratings, and Tolokers, and its Minesweeper advantage is negligible relative to reported variation. No statistical testing or robust ablation establishes that the Cauchy factorization, local filters, sparsification, or hierarchy are responsible for the results.

The runtime comparison is incomplete. The paper compares against dense eigendecomposition but not against stronger sparse/partial eigensolvers, approximate spectral methods, or end-to-end training/preprocessing costs. Memory use and numerical stability of long products of Cauchy factors are also not adequately evaluated.

Reproducibility is only partial. Hyperparameters are listed, but there is no clear code release statement, exact implementation details for the Cauchy solver are incomplete, baseline tuning/fairness is unclear, and key quantities such as parameter counts and ablation results are presented mainly through figures rather than detailed tables.

Some algorithms and proofs are too sketchy for the strength of the claims. For example, the secular equation pseudocode omits important edge cases such as repeated eigenvalues, deflation implementation details, and the final interlacing interval, while the appendix proof of the progressive identity largely appeals to prior work rather than giving a self-contained derivation.

The limitations and ethics discussion is minimal. The paper does not sufficiently discuss when the method becomes impractical, how sparsification may distort downstream predictions, or whether the method is only useful in transductive fixed-graph settings with substantial preprocessing.

strengths: The paper proposes an original and conceptually appealing bridge between rank-one spectral updates/Cauchy-like matrices and scalable spectral GNNs. The local-to-global factorization viewpoint is interesting and could be useful beyond the specific architecture.

The contribution is significant for spectral graph learning: it targets a real bottleneck of GFT-based GNNs, namely cubic eigendecomposition cost and lack of locality, and gives a plausible divide-and-conquer route with O(k n^2) dependence under small interfaces.

The empirical results are encouraging. On long-range heterophilous benchmarks, L2G-Net is competitive with strong baselines, slightly best on Minesweeper, close to Polynormer/Stable-ChebNet elsewhere, and uses far fewer learnable parameters than transformer-style models.

The synthetic experiments directly test the claimed scaling with graph size and interface size, and the reported runtime comparisons against dense eigendecomposition support the practical value of the factorization in favorable regimes.

Presentation is generally clear: the paper motivates the spectral/locality tradeoff well, gives algorithms, includes hyperparameter tables, and explains how sparsification and partitioning are used in practice.
weaknesses: Some central theoretical arguments need tightening. The proof of the progressive decomposition identity and deflation extension is quite terse, contains sign/notation inconsistencies between Lemma 3.1 and Theorem D.1, and does not fully justify the arbitrary-degeneracy case at the level expected for a main theoretical claim.

The sparsification discussion appears overclaimed. Theorem 4.1 and its proof conflate global spectral sparsification guarantees with independently sparsifying interfaces, and the stated construction/runtime and per-interface edge bounds are not convincingly derived. The downstream O(epsilon) spectral-layer error statement is also asserted rather than proved for the actual learned filters and normalized Laplacian setting.

Algorithmic details have rough edges that affect soundness and reproducibility: Algorithm 3 omits the final secular interval for the largest eigenvalue, does not clearly handle multiplicities/deflation, and the cost analysis mixes dense Cauchy operations, update propagation, and parallelism in a way that is hard to audit.

The real-world evaluation is positive but not fully convincing as evidence of broad superiority. The method is mostly competitive rather than clearly state-of-the-art, is tested on only four transductive datasets with one-level partitions, and lacks ablations on partition quality, sparsification ratio, hierarchy depth, local versus global filters, and preprocessing/storage costs.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The appendix gives useful hyperparameters and dataset statistics, but I did not see a code release, exact split/seed protocol, full implementation details for numerical solvers, or enough information to reproduce the Cauchy factorization robustly under degeneracies.

The paper has no explicit limitations or ethics/broader-impact discussion. The ethical risk seems low, but limitations such as dependence on favorable partitions, numerical stability of repeated rank-one secular solves, memory cost of storing dense factors, and behavior under aggressive sparsification should be discussed more directly.

strengths: The paper proposes an interesting and potentially useful bridge between divide-and-conquer eigenvalue methods and spectral GNNs: representing the GFT through a sequence of Cauchy-like factors associated with graph partitions and bridge edges. The local-to-global architectural idea is conceptually appealing and well aligned with long-range graph learning problems.

The manuscript contains substantial theoretical development, including treatment of repeated eigenvalues via deflation and an expressiveness argument showing that inserting local filters between Cauchy factors can represent operators beyond ordinary global spectral filters.

The empirical section is broad: it includes synthetic scaling studies, heterophilous transductive benchmarks, LRGB peptide tasks, and very large City-Networks graphs. The method is competitive in several settings while using relatively few learnable parameters.

The paper discusses important practical dimensions beyond accuracy, including factorization time, memory usage, end-to-end training time, learned filters, and attribution/locality analyses. Hyperparameters and dataset statistics are included in the appendix, which helps reproducibility.
weaknesses: Several central theoretical claims appear overstated or insufficiently justified. In particular, Theorem 4.1 claims interface sparsification can reduce each cut to O(epsilon^-2) edges while preserving the global Laplacian quadratic form for arbitrary graphs. Standard spectral sparsification bounds generally scale with graph size or effective dimension, and the manuscript does not justify why a size-independent per-interface bound is valid. This matters because bounded cut size is key to the claimed scalability for arbitrary graphs.

There is a mismatch between the theory and experiments: most theory is for the combinatorial/generalized Laplacian under rank-one edge updates, but experiments use the normalized Laplacian while sparsifying with the combinatorial Laplacian. Adding an edge to a normalized Laplacian also changes degree normalizations, so it is not obviously the same rank-one update model. The appendix asserts this carries over “up to a change of basis,” but this is not proven at the level needed for the algorithmic and exactness claims.

The stated O(kn^2) complexity is not fully supported by the appendix. Appendix F derives additional terms involving k^2 and fast Cauchy multiplication assumptions, then says the observed behavior is closer to O(kn^2). This weakens the main theoretical runtime claim, especially since practical implementations may not realize the required structured Cauchy multiplication guarantees.

The manuscript repeatedly describes the factorization as exact, but the practical large-graph method relies on cut sparsification, which makes the graph and its spectrum approximate. The empirical results do not sufficiently isolate the accuracy/runtime tradeoff as a function of sparsification error, nor do they compare predictions on the original graph versus the sparsified graph in a way that validates the claimed O(epsilon) filter-output deviation.

The experimental gains are modest. On Platonov et al. benchmarks, L2G-Net is close to but usually below Polynormer and not clearly better than strong spectral/SSM baselines except on Minesweeper. On peptides, it is not best overall and improves mainly over some spectral baselines. On City-Networks, it is competitive but not consistently best. This is useful, but the empirical evidence does not fully compensate for the theoretical uncertainties.

The comparison to eigendecomposition can be somewhat misleading: direct dense ED is a weak baseline for large sparse graphs, while partial/truncated spectral methods and established sparse eigensolver/divide-and-conquer implementations are not deeply benchmarked. The projected ED times for City-Networks are especially speculative and should not be treated as strong empirical evidence.

Reproducibility is only moderate. Hyperparameters are listed, but the paper does not provide enough implementation detail to verify the Cauchy factorization solver, numerical stability thresholds, exact sparsification implementation, baseline tuning parity, or whether all reported times include comparable preprocessing and data movement costs. Code availability is not stated.

Presentation is generally clear, but some claims are stronger than the evidence supports, including statements about exact scalable spectral processing on arbitrary graphs, locality/interpretablity advantages from Grad-CAM, and bounded-cut sparsification. A more careful limitations section would improve trust; the impact statement is generic and does not engage with possible misuse or dataset/domain-specific concerns.

strengths: The paper identifies an interesting connection between graph Laplacian edge insertions, rank-one eigenproblem updates, and Cauchy-like factors. This is a potentially useful lens for structured spectral graph algorithms.

The proposed L2G-Net architecture is conceptually coherent: inserting learnable local spectral filters between hierarchical merge factors is a plausible way to combine local and global spectral processing.

The empirical section covers several graph-learning settings, including heterophilous transductive graphs, LRGB peptide tasks, and large City-Networks graphs, and reports runtime and memory in addition to accuracy.
The method appears parameter-efficient relative to large attention-based baselines, and the paper includes some useful implementation details and hyperparameters in the appendix.
weaknesses: The central theoretical guarantees are not sufficiently supported. In particular, the claimed interface sparsification theorem states that each interface can be reduced to O(epsilon^-2) edges independent of interface size while preserving the global Laplacian quadratic form. This is not a standard consequence of Spielman-Srivastava sparsification and appears false in general; spectral sparsifiers typically require size depending on the number of vertices/effective dimension. This undercuts the scalability story for arbitrary graphs.

The paper repeatedly blurs exact and approximate claims. The Cauchy factorization may be exact for a chosen graph and hierarchy, but the large-scale experiments rely on aggressive sparsification of cuts, so the resulting transform is no longer the exact GFT of the original graph. Claims such as making exact spectral processing feasible at large scale are therefore misleading.

There are important gaps and inconsistencies in the theory. The sign convention differs between the main lemma and appendix theorem; Algorithm 2 has an undefined interval for the final secular root; the normalized Laplacian used in experiments is not handled rigorously by the edge-wise rank-one update theory because normalization changes degrees; and the proofs often cite deflation or prior rank-one results without establishing the stated arbitrary-graph claims in adequate detail.

The complexity and memory analysis is not fully convincing. The method still has O(kn^2)-type costs and dense structured operations; the paper does not clearly separate one-time factorization, per-layer forward cost, training cost, and preprocessing cost. Some reported training times show L2G-Net is slower than several baselines, weakening the practical efficiency claim.

The empirical gains are modest. On the heterophilous benchmark, L2G-Net is generally close to but not better than Polynormer and only marginally improves some spectral baselines. On peptides, it is below the best reported GNN/PE methods. On City-Networks, results are competitive but not consistently best. This does not justify the paper's stronger claims about state-of-the-art competitiveness.

Runtime comparisons are not sufficiently fair or informative. The main baseline is full dense eigendecomposition, including extrapolated O(n^3) times for large graphs, rather than strong numerical linear algebra baselines, approximate spectral methods, truncated eigensolvers, or optimized divide-and-conquer/HSS solvers. The extrapolated ED numbers in particular are weak evidence.

Key ablations are missing or underdeveloped: effect of hierarchy depth, partition quality, cut sparsification ratio, approximation error versus accuracy, exact versus sparsified factorization, and sensitivity to numerical degeneracies. These are central to the method's claimed advantages.

Reproducibility is only partial. Hyperparameters are listed, but the manuscript does not provide enough detail about code availability, baseline tuning, hardware/software implementations, or the full partition/sparsification pipeline to reliably reproduce the most important claims.

The limitations and ethics discussion is thin. The impact statement is generic, and the limitations discussion acknowledges that linear-time methods may be preferable at large scale but does not adequately confront the approximation/exactness issue or the cases where favorable small-cut hierarchies do not exist.

strengths: The paper develops an interesting and potentially useful connection between rank-one Laplacian updates, Cauchy-like eigenvector rotations, and hierarchical graph partitions. The local-to-global factorization is conceptually elegant and gives a clear architectural motivation for L2G-Net.

The contribution is broader than a model tweak: it includes a theoretical factorization, a partitioning/sparsification strategy, an expressivity argument, and experiments on both synthetic scaling tests and long-range graph benchmarks.

The empirical results are generally solid. L2G-Net is competitive on heterophilous and long-range datasets, often matching strong baselines with far fewer learned parameters, and the synthetic timing experiments support the claimed dependence on graph size and cut size.

The paper is well written overall. The figures and tables make the method easy to follow, and the appendix provides useful details on degeneracies, hyperparameters, sparsification, runtime, memory, and additional benchmark results.

The limitations are treated reasonably honestly: the conclusion notes that linear-time message passing or polynomial filters remain preferable when strict large-scale linear complexity is required, and the experiments include cases where L2G-Net is slower per epoch than simpler GNNs.
weaknesses: A central theoretical claim around interface sparsification appears under-justified. Theorem 4.1 claims each interface can be sparsified to k' <= O(epsilon^-2) while preserving the global Laplacian quadratic form, but standard spectral sparsification bounds usually scale with the number of vertices/effective dimension, e.g. O(n log n / epsilon^2). The paper does not provide enough argument for a dimension-free per-interface edge bound, and this matters because sparsification is key to making the method practical on real graphs.

The distinction between exact factorization of the original graph and approximate factorization after cut sparsification is sometimes blurred. Many real experiments rely on aggressive sparsification, e.g. keeping only one crossing edge for several Platonov datasets, so the model is no longer using the exact GFT of the original graph. The approximation error is only discussed at a high level through Lipschitz spectral-filter stability, without task-level or ablation evidence showing how much accuracy depends on sparsification strength.

The complexity analysis is not fully convincing as presented. The main text states O(k n^2), while the appendix includes additional k^2 terms and relies on fast structured Cauchy matrix-vector multiplication assumptions. Algorithm 2 explicitly constructs dense Cauchy matrices, and the paper does not sufficiently reconcile the algorithmic pseudocode, implementation, memory accounting, and asymptotic claims.

The empirical gains are meaningful but not decisive across all benchmarks. On the Platonov suite the method is close to, but often below, Polynormer; on City-Networks it is competitive but not consistently best; on peptides it trails the strongest reported GNN/PE variants. Thus the significance is more in the spectral factorization framework than in clear state-of-the-art performance.

The partitioning strategy is heuristic and graph-dependent, but its stability and sensitivity are not deeply studied. Different partitions or merge orders can yield different architectures, and the paper would benefit from ablations over hierarchy depth, sparsification ratio, partition quality, and failure cases on graphs without favorable small-cut structure.

Reproducibility is adequate but incomplete. The paper reports hyperparameters and hardware, but I did not see an explicit code-release statement, random seed protocol for all experiments, or enough implementation detail to reproduce the Cauchy/secular solver behavior and sparsification pipeline with confidence.
